own_scenes.desc: La primavera de 1966 trajo discos que respiraban apertura, y algunos de los más imaginativos los cantaban mujeres. «Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog» de Norma Tanega (febrero de 1966), producido por Herb Bernstein para Bob Crewe, mezclaba folk y bajo Motown, filosofía y ritmo go-go: una mujer que pasea sola y sin miedo por Nueva York, tan moderna y alusiva como Dylan. Tanega, pintora licenciada y camarera de campamento en los Catskills, se vio de pronto en una gira de seis semanas como única mujer (se cambiaba en un establo) y después en Londres, donde vivió con Dusty Springfield. Nancy Sinatra, con Lee Hazlewood, mezclaba Las Vegas, Los Ángeles, fantasía sadomaso y venganza femenina. Tras los Beatles, el pop británico había quedado dominado por hombres y las cantantes iban juntas en un mismo reportaje: Helen Shapiro no sobrevivió al Merseybeat; Cilla Black (Epstein, versiones de Bacharach/David), Sandie Shaw (una chica Biba descalza, fría y dueña de su imagen, que en «Nothing Comes Easy» canta a una acosadora) y Marianne Faithfull (elegida por su aspecto por Andrew Loog Oldham y arrojada a las giras) eran pioneras por el simple hecho de actuar.

refs.q: ‘Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog’ had an impact beyond its chart placings
refs.para: ‘Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog’ had an impact beyond its chart placings: it was one of those records that made people sit up and take notice. Norma became a star with her first single. Invited onto nationwide television, she initially came across like Joan Baez, a severe folk singer, but she played an electric guitar and shook a pair of big earrings designed by Kenneth Jay Lane. On her face was a look of amusement and total surprise. ‘It was shock. And awe,’ she says now about her unexpected fame.
refs.chapter: Mayo: Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog: la mística de la feminidad y la independencia femenina

refs.q: The language of pop was expanding, and women were the beneficiaries as well as men.
refs.para: The language of pop was expanding, and women were the beneficiaries as well as men. At the time, Tanega did not ally herself with any overt women’s politics. ‘I was a creator,’ she retorts when the word ‘feminism’ is mentioned. ‘That was never a question for me. It didn’t matter.’ Yet ‘Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog’ and its follow-up, ‘A Street That Rhymes at 6 A.M.’, were but two of several pop records that, during the first half of 1966, broke the mould of what women could sing about, and indeed could be.
refs.chapter: Mayo: Walkin’ My Cat Named Dog: la mística de la feminidad y la independencia femenina

refs.q: Sandie Shaw was even more one of the audience, a Biba girl stepping out from the street onto the stage.
refs.para: Sandie Shaw was even more one of the audience, a Biba girl stepping out from the street onto the stage. She was seventeen when she had her first #1, ‘There’s Always Something There to Remind Me’, another Bacharach/David cover. Ably guided by Adam Faith’s manager Eve Taylor, she enjoyed a sequence of big hits throughout 1964/5: ‘Message Understood’, ‘I’ll Stop at Nothing’ and her second #1, ‘Long Live Love’.
